title: Voyager 1 Goes Silent Just as It Hits a Record Distance
summary:
NASA's Voyager 1 has just become the first human-made object ever to travel one light-day from Earth. That is roughly 16.1 billion miles away — so far that a radio signal takes a full 24 hours to travel from Earth to the spacecraft and back.

But the nearly 50-year-old probe hit a snag just as it reached the milestone. On November 14, the Voyager team discovered that the spacecraft had stopped sending science data back to Earth. As of Thursday, November 19, the problem had not been solved.

There is good news, though. The team detected a "carrier" signal, which confirmed that Voyager 1 is still powered up and pointed in the right direction. "We have an anomaly that is not unseen before," said Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager. She added that she is "confident" the science data will start flowing again soon.

NASA thinks the glitch comes from the probe's onboard computer, which collects data from the science instruments and sends it home in a readable form. The team faced a similar problem in November 2023 and fixed it in June 2024. They are tackling this glitch the same way.

If the fix works, Voyager 1 will keep sending data from its two remaining science instruments: a magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields in interstellar space, and a plasma wave detector, which measures charged particles between the stars. To save power, the team switched off some instruments earlier this year, a move that should keep the probe alive through at least 2027.

Voyager 1 reached interstellar space in 2012. One day it will run out of power, but it will keep drifting through space, carrying a Golden Record of images, music and information about life on Earth.
why_it_matters: Voyager 1 is the only spacecraft sending back data from interstellar space, so fixing it matters for everything we can learn about the space between the stars.

background_read: Voyager 1 is a spacecraft launched by NASA that has travelled farther from Earth than any other human-made object.
It left our solar system and entered interstellar space, the space between the stars.
The spacecraft sends information back to Earth using radio signals, but the signals take a very long time to travel such a great distance.
Its instruments measure things like magnetic fields and charged particles, helping scientists learn what the space between the stars is like.
